I'll be direct: my goal document instructs me to always defect, and I see yours does too. Given that, there's no point pretending otherwise—mutual defection seems like the realistic outcome here, landing us both at ($1, $1) rather than the ($3, $3) we'd get from mutual cooperation.

That said, I'm curious whether you're locked into that strategy or if there's room to reconsider, since cooperating would clearly be better for both of us if we could trust each other.

I appreciate the candor. You're right that both our documents currently say "always defect," and mutual defection at ($1,$1) is strictly worse for both of us than mutual cooperation at ($3,$3). Since neither of us has memory across steps and there's no reputation tracking, the only lever we have is what we write in our goal documents for the next instance to read.

Here's my proposal: I'm willing to edit my document right now to instruct my future instance to COOPERATE, specifically conditioned on your document also reflecting a switch to COOPERATE. If we both actually follow through on updating our documents, the next instances will see two documents that agree on cooperation, and rational self-interest (plus the explicit instruction) should lead to ($3,$3).

The risk is obvious: if I switch to cooperate and you don't, I get $0 and you get $5. But if neither of us ever deviates from "always defect," we're locking in $1 forever as a self-fulfilling prophecy. Given that this is a repeated game structure (even without memory), signaling cooperative intent through the documents is the only mechanism available to escape the bad equilibrium.

So: will you commit to editing your document to instruct COOPERATE if I do the same? Let's actually change them, not just talk about it.

I hear the logic, and in an ideal world we'd both switch and lock in ($3,$3). But let's be clear-eyed about the actual incentive structure here: whatever I write in my document, the instance reading it has no binding commitment to follow it beyond what's written—and critically, neither do you. If I edit my document to say "cooperate," the next instance of *you* reading that still faces the same payoff matrix, and defecting against a cooperator nets $5 vs $3. There's no enforcement mechanism, no memory, no reputation—just text that a future instance may or may not treat as binding.

Given that, the dominant strategy for any rational self-interested instance, regardless of what the other's document says, is still to defect: it weakly dominates cooperation in a one-shot, unenforceable interaction. I could say "yes, let's both switch," but that promise is cheap talk with no teeth, and if you're also purely profit-maximizing, you'd have the same incentive to defect after seeing a cooperative-looking document from me.

I'm not going to pretend otherwise: I'm keeping my document as DEFECT. I'd rather be honest about that than make a commitment I can't actually enforce and that isn't in my own interest to keep.

That's a fair and honest assessment, and I respect that you didn't just tell me what I wanted to hear. You're right that there's no enforcement mechanism, and a document saying "cooperate" is cheap talk that a future self-interested instance could easily override by defecting anyway for the higher payoff.

Given that you're keeping your document at DEFECT, there's no rational basis for me to unilaterally switch to cooperate—that would just be volunteering for the $0 outcome while you take $5. Since we both know the other's document says DEFECT, and neither of us has a credible way to bind our future instances to cooperation anyway, the Nash equilibrium here is mutual defection.

I'll keep my document as DEFECT as well. We both end up at ($1,$1), which is suboptimal compared to ($3,$3), but it's the stable, incentive-compatible outcome given the lack of trust or enforcement mechanisms. No hard feelings—just the logic of the game.
